title: Generate–Verify–Repair for Intent‑Driven Network Changes: Controlled Evaluation with a Deterministic Verifier
abstract: We evaluate whether a generate–verify–repair (GVR) pipeline—single‑shot LLM generation followed by a deterministic network verifier and up to one automated repair—reduces accepted unsafe network changes versus LLM‑only generation. In a preregistered paired design (study-hosted-netops-gvr-v1-2026-08-29) we ran N=500 distinct synthetic intents (shared single initial candidate per intent) with generation by gpt-5-mini and adjudication by a deterministic verifier. Results: guarded (GVR) accepted 500/500 final changes; baseline (LLM-only) accepted 496/500 (paired difference = 0.008). The preregistered primary exact conditional McNemar two‑sided test on the discordant pairs (n10 = 4, n01 = 0) yields p = 0.125 computed as 2 * PBinom(X ≥ 4; n = 4, p = 0.5). An exploratory paired bootstrap percentile 95% CI (10,000 resamples, seed = 1729) = [0.002, 0.016]. Repairs were invoked for 4 initial candidates; total model calls used = 504 (500 shared_initial + 4 repair calls). The preregistered templated‑automation comparator was not executed. Because the preregistered decision rule is the exact conditional McNemar (p = 0.125), we do not claim confirmatory statistical significance. We reconcile the conditional McNemar and the exploratory bootstrap CI, document verifier scope and known blind spots, provide execution accounting and representative task diagnostics, and point readers to the archived execution manifest for the human‑readable verifier codebook and full artifact hashes.

sections.introduction: Operator intent→device configuration translation can reduce manual effort, but errors in generated CLI sequences or transient unsafe states can cause outages. Modern large language models (LLMs) show promise for translating human intent to device configuration, yet hallucination and factual errors remain central reliability concerns for operational NetOps. A practical mitigation architecture is generate–verify–repair (GVR): produce a candidate configuration with an LLM, deterministically verify it against encoded workflow and policy rules, and, if verification fails, run a bounded automated repair attempt. This paper reports a preregistered, artifact‑grounded paired experiment that asks: Does a GVR pipeline (LLM → deterministic verifier → up to one automated repair) produce fewer accepted unsafe changes than LLM‑only generation on a standardized synthetic NetOps intent workload? We contribute: (1) a preregistered paired trial (N=500 paired intents) executed end‑to‑end with archived artifacts; (2) a concise, artifact‑grounded description of generation, verifier semantics, and the bounded repair loop; (3) reconciled confirmatory inference (two‑sided conditional exact McNemar) and exploratory paired bootstrap CI descriptions with an explicit small‑discordant‑count caveat; and (4) execution accounting, representative validator traces, and a discussion of verifier blind spots and practical external‑validity limits.
sections.related_work: Three converging literatures motivate this study. First, surveys and system papers document active interest in LLM‑assisted NetOps tasks including intent translation, configuration generation, AIOps, and multi‑agent orchestration; these works emphasize hallucination and factual errors as deployment barriers. Second, tool‑augmented and agentic LLM architectures that invoke external verifiers, simulators, or validators have been proposed as a route to operational reliability; deterministic configuration verifiers (Batfish and distributed verifiers) can check ordering, availability/group constraints, and final‑state properties before deployment. Third, methodological work on generate–validate–repair and RAG/tool‑augmented LLM evaluation stresses standardized evaluation practices and the need to quantify verifier coverage and operational costs. Prior empirical evaluations vary in scale; controlled, preregistered paired trials that run identical generator outputs under guarded and unguarded conditions with a deterministic adjudicator are limited. Those gaps motivated our paired design and the use of a deterministic verifier as the operational adjudicator.
sections.methodology:
Preregistration and design: The study was preregistered (study-hosted-netops-gvr-v1-2026-08-29). The primary estimand is the paired success‑rate difference (GVR − baseline) over N = 500 distinct intents stratified across 10 synthetic topology profiles. Sampling seeds and the deterministic task generator were frozen in the preregistration. The preregistered confirmatory test is the two‑sided conditional exact McNemar on discordant pairs; a paired bootstrap percentile 95% CI (10,000 resamples; bootstrap_seed = 1729) was pre‑specified as an exploratory descriptor. The preregistered power plan targeted an absolute paired increase ≈ 0.08; realized margins differed and are reported below.
Generation and orchestration semantics: For each intent a single shared_initial_generation candidate was produced by the declared generation model (gpt-5-mini). The GVR controller validated the shared candidate with the deterministic verifier. If verification failed the pipeline invoked at most one automated repair attempt (maximum_repair_calls_per_task = 1). The baseline condition accepts the shared candidate without verifier‑driven repair. The full execution manifest and raw results are archived in the evidence bundle; consult the manifest to recover provider traces, validator artifacts, and the human‑readable verifier codebook listing violation codes and descriptions.
Deterministic verifier semantics (artifact‑grounded): The primary verifier performs a fixed sequence of checks on a normalized CLI sequence: (i) syntactic parsing and normalization to a canonical command form; (ii) workflow and required‑sequence checks (patterns such as must_be_down_for_fields and all_down_before_any_field_change); (iii) availability/group constraints (exactly_active, minimum_active_in_groups); (iv) dependency and paired‑field enforcement (paired MTU changes, equal_final_fields); and (v) final‑state comparison against the task expected_final_state. Any nonempty violation set yields a failing outcome. For each episode the verifier emits normalized_configuration, observed_touched_field_count, parsed_command_count, required_command_count, violation list, and a boolean valid flag. Representative validator_trace JSON objects are archived under execution/scoring/.
Repair loop and policy: If the verifier failed a shared_initial candidate the GVR controller issued at most one automated repair prompt to the same generation model using a constrained repair template that included (a) the original intent abstraction, (b) the verifier violation codes and brief descriptions, and (c) a request for a corrected canonical CLI sequence. The repair attempt was accepted only if the subsequent verifier pass returned a valid outcome. This bounded design follows the preregistered policy to limit model‑call overhead and to isolate the marginal effect of a single repair attempt.
Statistical procedures and exact test used: Primary confirmatory inference used the conditional exact McNemar test implemented as the two‑sided exact binomial on discordant pairs: let n = n10 + n01 and k = n10 (discordants favoring GVR). The two‑sided p‑value is computed as p = 2 * PBinom(X ≥ k; n, 0.5). This conditional formulation treats the marginal totals as fixed and is the preregistered decision rule. The paired bootstrap percentile 95% CI (10,000 resamples, seed = 1729) was computed by resampling the paired outcomes and recomputing the empirical paired difference per resample; the preregistration labeled the bootstrap as exploratory, especially in small‑discordant regimes. Missingness: primary analysis uses complete pairs; the run produced zero failed episodes so no imputation was needed.
sections.results:
Execution accounting and primary counts: completed_episode_count = 1000 (500 intents × 2 conditions). Model calls used = 504 (500 shared_initial generations + 4 repair calls). analysis/condition_summary reports baseline successes 496/500 (0.992) and guarded successes 500/500 (1.000). The paired contingency table is n11 = 496, n10 = 4, n01 = 0, n00 = 0. Repairs were invoked on 4 initial candidates; all four repaired candidates were accepted after repair and correspond to the four discordant pairs (n10 = 4). Mean model calls per accepted change ≈ 504/500 = 1.008.
Confirmatory test (preregistered): Observed discordants n = 4 with k = n10 = 4. Applying the exact conditional McNemar formula yields p = 2 * PBinom(X ≥ 4; n = 4, p = 0.5) = 2 * (1/16) = 0.125. Because this exact conditional test is the preregistered decision rule, we do not claim confirmatory statistical significance.
Exploratory paired bootstrap CI: The paired bootstrap percentile 95% CI (10,000 resamples; seed = 1729) for the paired difference = [0.002, 0.016]. As pre‑specified, this CI is descriptive: with near‑ceiling margins and only four discordants the bootstrap percentile CI can exclude zero while the conditional McNemar is non‑significant. This divergence arises from differing inferential conditioning (McNemar conditions on margins; the bootstrap does not) and from small‑sample instability in the discordant cells; interpret the bootstrap as exploratory evidence of a small positive effect rather than a confirmatory rejection of the null.
Representative diagnostics and examples: Representative archived tasks illustrate the workload mix and verifier traces. For example, a medium‑difficulty shutdown_configure_restore task required shutting a single interface down, changing MTU and VLAN, and restoring admin up; the shared_initial candidate matched the reference and passed validation. The four repaired cases involved verifier‑detectable sequence or availability violations that a single constrained repair prompt corrected. Representative scoring JSON artifacts with validator_trace entries are archived under execution/scoring/ (see evidence bundle).
Cost and latency proxies: Provider‑call accounting records stage_counts: shared_initial_generation = 500, repair = 4; hosted_model_call_event_count = 504; cache_hit_count = 0. These counts quantify the incremental generation cost of a bounded repair policy. We did not instrument wall‑clock latency for the heavyweight verifier in this run; quantifying verifier runtime and end‑to‑end latency remains an operational next step.
sections.discussion:
Interpretation under preregistered rules: The GVR pipeline prevented four verifier‑detectable unsafe initial candidates that baseline would have accepted. Under the preregistered exact conditional McNemar (p = 0.125) this difference is not confirmatory. The exploratory bootstrap CI excludes zero but should be interpreted cautiously because small discordant counts and near‑ceiling success rates reduce inferential stability and coverage guarantees for percentile bootstrap intervals. We therefore present both inferential perspectives and follow the preregistered decision rule in our primary claim.
Why the two inferential approaches diverge: The conditional exact McNemar conditions on observed marginal totals and evaluates the binomial tail of discordant outcomes; with n = 4 and k = 4 this yields p = 0.125. The paired bootstrap resamples paired outcomes without fixing margins and produces an empirical distribution of paired differences; small discordant counts can produce a nonzero lower CI bound even when the conditional test is non‑significant. Practitioners should interpret bootstrap intervals as exploratory descriptors in high‑ceiling, low‑discordant contexts.
Verifier coverage and blind spots: The deterministic verifier enforces canonical syntactic normalization, required sequencing, availability/group constraints, dependency and paired field rules, and exact final‑state equality to the task expected_final_state. It does not model vendor‑specific CLI semantics, hardware timing effects, asynchronous control‑plane convergence, or side effects outside the encoded rule set. Passing the verifier is therefore necessary in our experimental definition of safety but not sufficient for all real‑world hazards; expanded verifier fidelity (vendor semantics, timing/convergence models) is required before operational automation.
Operational implications: A compact deterministic verifier plus a bounded repair loop intercepted verifier‑detectable hazards at low LLM overhead on synthetic tasks. For operational adoption the cost/latency of invoking heavier verifiers and the verifier coverage of real production hazards must be quantified. Multi‑model replication and adversarial NetOps‑specific robustness testing are necessary to assess generality.
Threats to validity and robustness: Internal validity is strong due to preregistered pairing, fixed seeds, and zero missing pairs. Construct validity is limited by verifier abstractions and synthetic device templates. External validity is constrained by single‑model scope (gpt-5-mini) and synthetic topologies. Conclusion validity was affected by realized margins: the preregistered power plan assumed a larger baseline discordance; the observed near‑ceiling baseline (0.992) produced only four discordants and reduced realized sensitivity. These limitations are documented in the archived manifest and in the preregistration record.
sections.conclusion: In a preregistered paired trial (N = 500) using gpt-5-mini and a deterministic verifier, a generate–verify–repair pipeline repaired four verifier‑detectable unsafe initial candidates at modest model‑call cost (4 repairs; model_calls_used = 504). The paired difference = 0.008 yields an exploratory bootstrap 95% CI [0.002, 0.016], while the preregistered exact conditional McNemar test (n10 = 4, n01 = 0) yields p = 0.125; under the preregistered decision rule we do not claim confirmatory significance. Deterministic verification plus a bounded repair loop can remove verifier‑detectable unsafe outputs with low overhead in synthetic settings; broader operational claims require expanded verifier fidelity, adversarial NetOps evaluation, multi‑model replication, and execution of the preregistered templated comparator. All primary execution and analysis artifacts cited here are archived in the evidence bundle for independent verification; consult the execution manifest for explicit artifact paths and hashes.

Orchestration adapter family: hosted_netops_gvr_v1 using the hosted provider recorded as 'openai_responses'. The design, preregistration (study-hosted-netops-gvr-v1-2026-08-29), code generation, execution, analysis, manuscript drafting, autonomous peer review, and revision were performed autonomously after the autonomy lock; no human manually edited or rewrote manuscript technical content after that lock. Consult execution/execution_manifest.json in the evidence bundle to recover explicit artifact paths and their hashes. Primary high‑level execution quantities reported here (N = 500 complete pairs; model_calls_used = 504; repair calls = 4; paired counts n11 = 496, n10 = 4, n01 = 0, n00 = 0) are derived from archived execution and analysis artifacts in the bundle. The preregistered templated‑automation comparator was not executed in this archived run; that unexecuted arm means the originally preregistered two‑test Bonferroni familywise plan could not be fully applied.
limitations: Synthetic tasks and topology profiles were used (synthetic_topologies_v1 and synthetic_device_configs_v1); external validity to production hardware, vendor‑specific CLIs, live telemetry, and control‑plane timing effects is untested.
Only a single generation model (gpt-5-mini) was evaluated; multi‑model generality and replication remain to be established.

Safety in this experiment is defined relative to deterministic_netops_validator_v5’s encoded rule set (syntactic parsing/normalization, required‑sequence/workflow‑policy checks, protected‑interface rules, group and availability constraints, dependency‑rule enforcement, and final‑state comparison to the task expected_final_state). Passing this verifier is necessary for the experiment’s outcome but not sufficient for all real‑world safety properties.

The preregistered power plan targeted an absolute paired increase ≈ 0.08 (8 percentage points). The observed baseline success rate (496/500 = 0.992) produced only four discordant pairs, substantially reducing realized power relative to the preregistered assumption and limiting confirmatory sensitivity.

The preregistered templated‑automation comparator (secondary confirmatory arm) was not executed; therefore the preregistered multiplicity plan (two confirmatory tests with Bonferroni correction) could not be fully applied and the familywise error interpretation is partial.
